summary: Records that the Unicode Consortium deprecated the language tag characters described in RFC 2482 and recommends against their use, and moves RFC 2482 to Historic status to reduce the chance people use it.

eli5.summary: Some invisible characters were once proposed to label text with its language. Experts decided not to use them, so the old document was retired.

subtitle: Moving an outdated Unicode feature from standards to history.

tldr.problem: RFC 2482 described special Unicode characters for marking language tags in plain text, but the Unicode Consortium deprecated the facility and recommends against its use.
tldr.mechanism: This informational RFC announces that RFC 2482 has been moved to Historic status to discourage implementers from adopting the deprecated language tag mechanism.
tldr.outcome: The change reduces the chance that internet protocols will use the deprecated Unicode feature, guiding development toward better alternatives like MIME Content-Language headers or XML markup.

today: RFC 2482 is now Historic. Internet Standard and other formal specifications should use alternatives such as MIME Content-Language headers or XML markup for language identification.

sections.title: Why RFC 2482 is Being Deprecated
sections.content:
RFC 2482 proposed a mechanism for embedding special Unicode language tag characters into plain text to identify which language the text was written in. The idea was to enable language identification without requiring markup like XML.

The Unicode Consortium—the organization that maintains the Unicode Standard—has now deprecated this facility. They found that whole-message language identification (such as MIME Content-Language headers) and general markup mechanisms (such as XML) proved more practical. The language tag character approach was an idea whose time never quite came.
sections.eli5: A way to mark text's language with invisible characters didn't work well in practice, so it was retired.

sections.title: The Action Taken
sections.content: RFC 2482 has been reclassified as Historic. This designation means that Internet protocols and Standards-Track documents should no longer use the facilities it describes. The change removes an outdated mechanism from consideration and steers protocol designers toward better alternatives already in use.
sections.eli5: The old note is moved to a 'historic' pile so new protocols won't accidentally use the broken approach.

sections.title: Security Implications
sections.content: Deprecating RFC 2482 has a net positive security effect. The language tag character facility was no longer encouraged or supported by the Unicode Consortium, and it could have posed a slight risk if misinterpreted or if implementations had unsupported expectations of how it would work. Removing it eliminates that source of confusion and misconfiguration.
sections.eli5: Getting rid of the old, unsupported approach makes systems safer because people won't get confused trying to use something that doesn't really work.

references.text: Whistler, K. and G. Adams, "Language Tagging in Unicode Plain Text", RFC 2482, January 1999.
Alvestrand, H., "Content Language Headers", RFC 3282, May 2002.
